explain.say: Stopping distance is how far a car travels from the moment the driver sees danger to the moment it stops. It is two parts added together: the thinking distance and the braking distance.

explain.say: Thinking distance is covered during your reaction time, about two thirds of a second, so it grows in step with speed. At 30 miles per hour a car needs about 23 metres in total: 9 thinking and 14 braking.

faq.a: Thinking distance is how far the car travels while the driver reacts, before the brakes even start working. At 20 miles per hour it is about 6 metres, and it grows in step with speed.
asks: How far does a car take to stop at 20 mph?

faq.a: Braking distance is how far the car travels from when the brakes are applied until it stops. At 30 miles per hour it is about 14 metres, and it grows with the square of speed.
asks: How far does a car take to stop at 30 mph?

faq.q: Why does doubling speed quadruple braking distance?
faq.a: Movement energy is half the mass times the speed squared, so twice the speed means four times the energy. The brakes remove energy at about the same rate per metre, so they need about four times as far.
asks: Why is it four times longer at double the speed?

faq.a: Wet or icy roads, worn tyres or brakes, a heavy load, and a tired, distracted or drunk driver all make stopping distances longer. On ice, braking distance can be up to ten times longer.

faq.q: How far does a car take to stop at 70 miles per hour?
faq.a: The UK Highway Code gives about 96 metres at 70 miles per hour: 21 metres thinking and 75 metres braking, in good conditions.

facts: The UK Highway Code gives typical stopping distances of 23 metres at 30 mph and 96 metres at 70 mph.
The Highway Code warns that braking distances can be up to ten times longer on icy roads.
Braking distance grows with the square of speed, while thinking distance grows in step with speed.
